description: Fazari is a software and AI team from Sakarya, Türkiye, taking on the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. We are named after al-Fazari, the 8th-century Baghdad astronomer credited with building the first astrolabe in the Islamic world. Our goal is a modern astrolabe for a moving sky: a public web tool that blinks SPHEREx images taken months apart, so anyone can watch stars, asteroids and brown dwarfs move. Teammates with astronomy (FITS/WCS), Python, web or design skills are welcome.
summary: Pluto was found by "blinking" two photographs of the same sky and spotting the dot that jumped. Fazari brings that blink to NASA's SPHEREx, which maps the whole sky in 102 infrared wavelengths every six months. Type any coordinate or object name: the site reads only the needed parts of SPHEREx images from NASA/IPAC IRSA, removes the zodiacal background, masks bad pixels, blinks only matching wavelengths so a color change never looks like motion, and measures the motion with an error bar, calibrated on ESA Gaia stars. A one-line verdict says "moves", "no motion" or "not sure yet". All five challenge targets are measured: Barnard's Star moved 10.21" +/- 0.06" in 0.98 years; Gaia DR3 predicts 10.24". A verification page shows 13 numbered tests: 10 pass, 2 fail, 1 limit, failures included. We also recover known asteroids, measure three comets and Pluto, check 86 fast stars against Gaia, and searched for Planet X: no candidate, but an honest upper limit. English and Turkish. Every new find stays a candidate until checked. Named after al-Fazari, the 8th-century Baghdad astronomers credited with the first astrolabes of the Islamic world.
details:
THE STORY IN 30 SECONDS

Pluto was found with a "blink comparator": two photographs of the same sky, taken days apart, flipped back and forth until one dot was seen to jump. The same trick still works. Volunteers in NASA's Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 project blink infrared sky images in their browsers and have found brown dwarfs that computers missed. The search for a distant "Planet X" (today's hypothesized Planet Nine) is, at heart, the same search: something faint that moves.

NASA's SPHEREx observatory (launched on 11 March 2025) maps the entire sky in 102 infrared wavelengths (0.75 to 5 micrometers) and returns to every spot about every six months. That makes it a new blink machine for the whole sky. But its raw images are hard for non-experts to use: each image sees a different wavelength across its field, files are large, bright stars saturate, and even the fastest star moves less than two 6.15" pixels per year.

Fazari turns those images into something anyone can watch and trust: a blink of the same sky, at the same wavelength, on different dates, with a measurement and its error bar, checked against ESA's Gaia catalog, and a one-line verdict on top.

The name honors al-Fazari, a family of astronomers in 8th-century Baghdad who are traditionally credited with making the first astrolabes in the Islamic world. Their astrolabe measured the positions of a sky that seemed fixed. Fazari measures a sky that moves.

WHAT IT DOES

- The five challenge targets, measured from SPHEREx images (viewer page, one link per target):

- Barnard's Star: shift 2025-08 to 2026-08 (0.98 yr) 10.21" +/- 0.06"; Gaia DR3 predicts 10.24" (0.6 sigma). Proper motion from the joint fit of 335 exposures: 10.37 +/- 0.06"/yr. The candidate finder, not told where the star is, measured 10.361 +/- 0.051"/yr (test V1); Gaia DR3: 10.393"/yr.

- Epsilon Indi B: shift 2025-10 to 2026-09 (0.96 yr) 4.54" +/- 0.03"; Gaia DR3 predicts 4.56" (0.9 sigma). Found blind at 4.678 +/- 0.02"/yr; Gaia DR3: 4.684"/yr (test V2). Its infrared position is offset from Gaia by about +0.27" E, -0.53" N, the same in both telescope orientations; this is consistent with the unresolved binary.

- WISE 0855-0714 (not in Gaia): detected only at 4.0 and 4.6 micron. Shift 2025-05 to 2026-05 (0.99 yr) 8.42" +/- 0.56"; Kirkpatrick et al. 2021 predicts 8.03" (0.7 sigma). Found blind at 8.187 +/- 0.567"/yr; reference 8.152"/yr (test V4).

- RW Aurigae: brightness at 4.0 micron, 2025-09 to 2026-09: x0.504 +/- 0.035 (fades), while constant or brighter at 1-2 micron.

- R Draconis (Mira variable): brightness at 4.6 micron, 2025-06 to 2026-06: x0.516 +/- 0.028.

- Any point on the sky, with an error bar. In the sky explorer you type decimal or sexagesimal coordinates or an object name (CDS Sesame), or click the sky. The in-browser engine runs on the static site: it reads only the needed image regions from IRSA's public SPHEREx cloud bucket, cleans, aligns and stacks them, calibrates positions on Gaia DR3 field stars, and gives a blink, a measured motion with its error and the Gaia prediction. First answer in about 20 s, full result after. Example: Kapteyn's Star as a free point, measured in the browser at 8.665 +/- 0.163"/yr; Gaia DR3: 8.644"/yr. The local Python engine does more when it runs on the same computer: up to 30 exposures per season and wavelength bin, all six bins, the candidate finder and a quick "is it moving?" answer.

- Blink viewer: Blink, Step, Swipe and Trail modes; play/pause, speed, season choice, zoom; measured-motion arrow, Gaia marker, difference image (last minus first season); FLAGS layer for bad and saturated pixels; spectrum at the target; field of view 0.15-0.6 deg; coordinates in the URL. A one-line verdict on top of every result ("moves", "no motion" or "not sure yet"); a result without an error bar says "no motion can be stated". A guided tour explains the page step by step.

- Verification page: 13 numbered tests (V1-V13) with their evidence files. 10 pass, 2 fail, 1 reaches a limit, and the failures are shown, not hidden:

- V6 fail: fake movers added to real images; over two random seeds the best bin recovers 95.1 % (173 of 182), below our 99 % target.

- V12 fail: fast-star sweep; 81 of 86 stars agree with Gaia DR3 within 3 sigma, and the test needs all of them.

- V8 limit: known asteroids (below).

- Passed, for example: 4 of 4 known movers found without being told where they are (V9); 0 fake movers in 1,200 date shuffles across 12 fields (V7); parallaxes of 29 fast stars, measured from the same images, at 0.88 +/- 0.10 times Gaia DR3 (V13).

- Known asteroids: in 24 ecliptic SPHEREx fields, matched with IMCCE SkyBoT: 47 of 53 known asteroids found down to V 17, 101 of 132 to V 18, 205 of 451 to V 19; median offset 0.111 pixel; 96 false detections in total.

- Comets: three comets and Pluto, selected over all public SPHEREx images with JPL SBDB and Horizons, then measured in the SPHEREx pixels. 3I/ATLAS (interstellar comet) is found in 58 of 58 exposures, and its measured speed is within 0.002 % of the JPL Horizons ephemeris. Also C/2025 R2 (SWAN), C/2025 A6 (Lemmon) and Pluto as a labelled bonus. Known objects, not new ones.

- Fast-star sweep: before measuring, we wrote down 90 fast Gaia DR3 stars and one fixed method. 86 were measured (the 4 failures stay in the table). The typical star agrees with Gaia to 7 % (0.17"/yr; 5 % for the fastest 48). 81 of 86 are within 3 sigma, where 99.7 % would be ideal; the 5 misses are published by name.

- Planet X search: 15 strips on the predicted Planet Nine orbit (Brown & Batygin 2021) in three runs, 2,770 SPHEREx exposures. Run 1's rules were written down and frozen before the search (a second pass with two added checks was declared, not blind); runs 2 and 3 had their rules pushed to GitHub before their first image byte was read. Result: no candidate. With no candidate in the 4.99 square degrees of the blind runs 2 and 3, false alarms stay below 0.61 per square degree (95 %). Upper limit, measured with 11,000 injected fake planets: no body brighter than V 19.45 (50 % completeness; 90 %: V 18.10) between 350 and 500 AU in these strips (7.07 square degrees, 0.082 % of the predicted band). A planet of 2.07 Earth radii is that bright out to 262-365 AU, depending on how much light it reflects (20-75 %).

- English and Turkish on every page.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Find images. A static index of all SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 images tells both engines which images cover a point; the local engine falls back to the NASA/IPAC IRSA Simple Image Access (SIA) service. The pipeline downloads 0.2 deg cutouts; the browser reads only the needed rows from IRSA's public S3 bucket with HTTP range requests.

2. Seasons. Exposures are grouped into observing seasons wherever consecutive dates are more than 30 days apart.

3. Wavelength bins. SPHEREx uses a linear variable filter, so the wavelength changes across each detector. We read the wavelength at the target pixel from each image's spectral WCS and put exposures into bins at 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0 and 4.6 micron (+/-6 %). Each bin is tied to one detector (D1-D6), so a frame never mixes detectors and only matching wavelengths are blinked.

4. Cleaning. We subtract the ZODI (zodiacal light) model, mask bad pixels from the FLAGS layer and mark saturated pixels.

5. Blink frames. Exposures are reprojected onto one north-up grid centred on the target (3"/pixel) and median-stacked per season and bin. All frames of a bin share one stretch, so a brightness change in the animation is real.

6. Predicted position. The catalog position is moved to each exposure's time with proper motion, perspective acceleration where a radial velocity is known (Barnard's Star) and annual parallax from the Earth's position.

7. Detection check, before any position fit. The SPHEREx empirical PSF is fitted at the predicted position with neighbours fitted at the same time. A season counts as a detection at S/N >= 5. A target detected nowhere gets "not detected" and no motion numbers.

8. Calibration on Gaia DR3. In every exposure we measure unsaturated, isolated Gaia DR3 field stars and remove the offset per season and detector (278 reference stars around Barnard's Star).

9. Positions and motion. Bright, saturated targets: a fit to the unsaturated wings, then a joint fit of all exposures for position and proper motion, with one centroid offset per detector. Faint targets: one PSF position per season, errors from the fit and a bootstrap, then a weighted linear fit.

10. Brightness targets: in each exposure the target is divided by 2-5 comparison stars in the same image; the result is a ratio to the first season.

11. Candidate finder (v1.1): looks for anything in the whole field that moved or changed, checks it against star catalogs, parallax and known asteroids (SkyBoT), and reports a candidate, never a discovery.

12. Publish. The pipeline writes frames, GIFs, difference images and a metadata file that records the exact SPHEREx source files and carries an AI-disclosure field.

SCIENTIFIC VALIDATION

- Independent check: August 2025 vs August 2026. SPHEREx has the same orientation in both seasons, so detector-fixed offsets cancel. Barnard's Star: 10.21" +/- 0.06" at PA 355.7 deg; Gaia DR3 predicts 10.24" at PA 355.7 deg.

- Joint fit, Barnard's Star, 335 exposures: proper motion -810 +/- 56, 10336 +/- 56 mas/yr; Gaia DR3: -802, 10362 mas/yr. Per-exposure scatter 0.41", about 1/15 of a native pixel.

- A systematic we found and handle: Barnard's Star is saturated, so only the wings can be fitted. This leaves an offset fixed to the detector. SPHEREx turns about 180 deg between the August and March seasons, so the offset flips on the sky. Without the correction the 2025-08 to 2026-03 shift points at PA 20.1 deg; after it, 5.97 deg; Gaia DR3 predicts 5.93 deg. In one season the east offset from Gaia drops from 0.76" to 0.05".

- Not pulled toward Gaia: started from 4 wrong motions up to 1.039"/yr off, the Barnard measurement always returned within 0.0425"/yr of the true-start result (test V10). In the fast-star sweep, a start 10 % wrong moved the answer by well under 1 % of that error.

- No fake motion: 0 moving candidates in 6 fields with no known mover (V5); 0 fake movers in 1,200 date shuffles across 12 fields, 1,739,200 source trials (V7).

- Limits we state: every season of Barnard's Star is still about +0.13" N (+/-0.04") from Gaia DR3; this cancels in shifts and motions and is not yet understood.

WHAT CAN SPHEREx RESOLVE?

SPHEREx pixels are 6.15". Barnard's Star moves about 1.7 pixels per year; Epsilon Indi B less than one pixel. Both are still measured to a few hundredths of an arcsecond, because every season adds many exposures. In the fast-star sweep the smallest motion seen at 5 sigma is 0.64"/yr (median error 0.13"/yr per axis). Each result card states its own error; when there is no error bar, the page says no motion can be stated instead of showing noise.

WEB TOOL

- Static site (HTML/CSS/JavaScript, GitHub Pages, no server code, no login). Pages: sky explorer (Aladin Lite v3 sky with Gaia, WISE, 2MASS and SPHEREx layers), result viewer, blink for any point, verification page, asteroids, comets, Planet X, the story.

- Heavy work runs in a Web Worker in the browser. Offline tests run in GitHub Actions on every push.

- Live site: https://adembtr.github.io/fazari/. Code: https://github.com/adembtr/fazari (MIT license).

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Education: a teacher or student can open one link and see, with their own eyes, that "fixed" stars move, using fresh SPHEREx data from 2025-2026, and why Pluto was found the way it was.

- Trust: the blink comes with a measurement and its error bar, compared with Gaia, and a page of numbered tests that shows what fails. Users learn how scientists test a claim, not only what it looks like.

- Citizen science: in the spirit of Backyard Worlds: Planet 9, volunteers get an infrared, multi-wavelength blink for any point of the SPHEREx sky, with wavelength matching. A naive blink would show false "motion".

- Open: free, no login, MIT-licensed code; English and Turkish, so it also reaches students in Turkiye.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- Wavelength-matched blinking: we treat SPHEREx's linear variable filter as a design constraint and turn it into a feature. You can blink the same star at 1.0 micron or at 4.6 micron.

- A measurement, not just a picture: shift, error bar, Gaia prediction and a one-line verdict side by side, for any point on the sky, in the browser.

- We use SPHEREx's 180 deg seasonal turn as a tool: it separates a detector-fixed offset from true sky motion.

- Direction, not only speed: for Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B and WISE 0855-0714, both the speed and the direction we measure agree with the catalogue within one sigma.

- Live data, no dependence on IRSA's search services: every measurement reads the needed pixels live from IRSA's public SPHEREx bucket. When IRSA's search services were down on 15 November 2026, the site kept measuring.

- Pre-registered tests: the fast-star list and the first Planet X rules were written down before any pixel was measured, and the failures are published.

- An honest Planet X answer: no candidate, and a stated limit of what this search could have seen.

- The identity: a 1,200-year-old story of sky instruments from our part of the world, retold for a moving sky.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Python (astropy, reproject, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib, Pillow, healpy), uv; HTML, CSS, JavaScript (Web Workers), Aladin Lite v3; GitHub, GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages; NASA/IPAC IRSA SIA, cutout and TAP services and the public SPHEREx S3 bucket; ESA Gaia Archive and CDS VizieR; CDS Sesame and SIMBAD; IMCCE SkyBoT; JPL Horizons and SBDB.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific honesty: we call a result independent only if it truly is. Systematics, saturation, failures and unresolvable cases are reported, not hidden. Every new object is a candidate until checked.

- Validity: wavelength matching, one detector per bin, background subtraction, bad-pixel and saturation handling, per-detector offsets, calibration on Gaia DR3 field stars, parallax as well as proper motion in the prediction, error bars on every motion.

- Data volume and cost: only the needed image regions are read, so it runs on a laptop or a phone; a static site is free to host.

- Reproducibility: the pipeline re-runs from the public archive with the commands in the README; the metadata file records the exact SPHEREx source files for every frame.

- Accessibility: no login, no installation, phone layout, simple and detailed views, clear labels, shareable links, two languages.

- Credit and rights: all data are credited, with DOIs where they exist; no NASA logos or branding are used; the AI-generated team logo carries a visible label.

WHAT WE CANNOT DO (YET)

- Two of our 13 tests fail. Injection test (V6): over two random seeds the best bin recovers 95.1 % of fake movers (173 of 182), below our 99 % target. Fast-star sweep (V12): 5 of 86 stars are more than 3 sigma from Gaia DR3; 8 stars have fits with no degrees of freedom left, and two (LAWD 37, Ross 578) come out about 22 % slow.

- Barnard's Star is saturated: its position comes from the wings, and every season is still about +0.13" N from Gaia DR3 (not yet understood).

- WISE 0855-0714 is faint for SPHEREx: its season positions have 0.2-0.45" errors, and the Gaia field-star calibration is not applied to it.

- Brightness changes of saturated stars come from the PSF wings; treat them as indicative, not as calibrated light curves. R Draconis has no value at 4.0 micron.

- The detection threshold and the noise calibration are empirical.

- The Planet X search covered 0.082 % of the predicted band; it says nothing about the rest.

- The spectrum is measured at the target position, not yet at any clicked pixel. The sky index is rebuilt with one command, not yet on a schedule. The browser engine does not run the candidate finder.

- Next: an index of moving and changing points that updates with every new SPHEREx season.

USE OF AI

Code, tests and documentation were written with help from Anthropic's Claude (Claude Code; Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2 models), which was also used for code review and research notes. Commits made with AI help carry a "Co-Authored-By: Claude" line. The sky images and measurements are computed from NASA SPHEREx data by our code, not by an AI model. Team Fazari designed the project and checked and tested the results. The team logo was generated with Google Gemini; it is not in the repository or on the site, and every copy shown is visibly labelled as AI-generated (a watermark on the project-page image, a watermark and a caption on the slides). AI use is also stated in the README, on the site (Credits panel and page footers) and in every result file. No NASA logos or branding are used.
